lead: The link power budget is a single addition. It adds every loss and margin between the transmitter and the receiver, then compares the total with the power difference available. The idea exists because a link must still work after connectors age, splices add loss and the laser weakens. It is used at design time to choose the source, fiber, connector count and receiver, and to leave a clear spare margin. If the sum fits, the link closes; if not, the design changes.
prereq: You need: 5.1 for the five-block link chain, Unit 2 for fiber loss mechanisms, and Unit 3 for connector and splice losses.

blocks.text: Start with the transmitter mean launched power P_T in dBm and the receiver sensitivity P_R in dBm. The difference P_T − P_R is the power you can afford to lose, in dB. Put every loss and reserve on the right side. The budget equation is:
P_T − P_R = αL + α_c N_c + α_s N_s + M
blocks.where: P_T is mean launched power in dBm; P_R is receiver sensitivity in dBm; α is fiber attenuation in dB/km; L is fiber length in km; α_c is loss per connector in dB; N_c is the number of connectors; α_s is loss per splice in dB; N_s is the number of splices; M is the system margin in dB.

blocks.text: The left side is a power difference in dB. Every term on the right is a loss in dB. A positive M is an allowance for ageing, temperature, repairs and extra connectors; it is not a measured loss. The budget closes when the right side is less than or equal to the left. The actual received power is P_T minus the physical losses only. The margin is then held back as reserve.

Do not add a dBm value to a dB value. P_T and P_R are absolute powers in dBm; αL, α_cN_c, α_sN_s and M are ratios in dB. The received power in dBm is P_T − αL − α_cN_c − α_sN_s. Compare that with P_R; the difference is the headroom. Of that headroom, M is reserved as margin and the rest is spare.

sections.h3: Typical values and the extra penalty

blocks.text: Use planning values, not the best laboratory number. Typical values are:

A connector count includes both ends and every patch panel in the path. A splice count counts joints inside the span; a 60 km span spliced every 10 km has five splices, not six, unless the ends are spliced to pigtails. System margin is commonly 4–6 dB. For a short indoor link a smaller margin may be acceptable; for an outdoor span use the larger end.

Sensitivity is the minimum usable power at the required bit error rate. Overload is the maximum power the receiver can accept before it saturates. The budget must satisfy P_R ≤ received power ≤ P_overload. A very short link with a strong laser can fail from overload; add a fixed attenuator. A link near its dispersion limit also needs extra power because spreading pulses close the eye. This dispersion power penalty P_d is in dB and is added as one more loss term: P_T − P_R = αL + α_cN_c + α_sN_s + M + P_d.

sections.h3: Design rule and reading the result

blocks.text: Compute in this order: fiber loss, connector loss, splice loss, system margin. Then subtract from available power. Spare = (P_T − P_R) − (αL + α_cN_c + α_sN_s + M). A positive spare means the budget closes. A negative spare means it does not; reducing M to make it fit is not design, it is hiding risk. Change a real term: shorter L, lower-loss fiber, fewer splices, better connectors, a higher-power source, or a more sensitive receiver. Each change has a cost.

The design rule is economic: pick the cheapest source and fiber that still close the budget with a sensible margin. An 850 nm multimode LED link is often cheapest for a building; a 1310 nm single-mode link fits medium distances; a 1550 nm single-mode laser fits long spans. After the loss budget closes, check the rise-time budget in 5.3. Loss decides reach; rise time decides speed. The shorter limit wins.
A spare margin is useful, but too much spare can mean you paid for a laser or fiber you did not need. Keep enough margin for repairs and ageing, and no more than the link economics justify.

examples.question: Design a 2.5 Gb/s point-to-point link: a 1550 nm laser with 0 dBm mean launched power, 60 km of single-mode fiber with α = 0.22 dB/km, two connectors at 0.5 dB each, one splice every 10 km at 0.1 dB each, receiver sensitivity −28 dBm at 2.5 Gb/s, and a 6 dB system margin. Does the budget close? Find the spare margin and the worst-case received power.
steps: Count splices inside the 60 km span: 60/10 − 1 = 5 splices. The two end connections are connectors, not splices.
Add system margin: total budget used = 14.7 + 6 = 20.7 dB.
Headroom above sensitivity = −14.7 − (−28) = 13.3 dB. Of this, 6 dB is reserved margin, leaving 7.3 dB spare.
examples.answer: Yes: total used = 20.7 dB, available = 28 dB, spare = 7.3 dB, and worst-case received power = −14.7 dBm, which is above the −28 dBm sensitivity.
examples.check:
def main():
    L = 60
    alpha = 0.22
    Nc = 2
    ac = 0.5
    Ns = L // 10 - 1
    a_s = 0.1
    M = 6.0
    PT = 0.0
    PR = -28.0
    fiber = L * alpha
    connectors = Nc * ac
    splices = Ns * a_s
    physical = fiber + connectors + splices
    used = physical + M
    available = PT - PR
    spare = available - used
    rx = PT - physical
    headroom = rx - PR
    print(f'{fiber:.1f}')
    print(f'{connectors:.1f}')
    print(f'{splices:.1f}')
    print(f'{M:.1f}')
    print(f'{used:.1f}')
    print(f'{available:.1f}')
    print(f'{spare:.1f}')
    print(f'{rx:.1f}')
    print(f'{headroom:.1f}')

if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

traps: Adding a dBm power to a dB loss. Keep P_T, sensitivity and received power in dBm; keep losses and margins in dB.
Forgetting the system margin or one connector. Count both ends and every patch panel; margin is a real budget line, not optional.
Miscounting splices: a 60 km span spliced every 10 km has five splices inside, not six, unless the ends are spliced to pigtails.
Confusing sensitivity with overload. Sensitivity is the minimum usable power; overload is the maximum. A short link can fail from too much power.
Leaving out the dispersion power penalty when the link is near its dispersion limit; it behaves like one more dB loss in the budget.

quiz.q: Write the link power-budget equation and give the unit of each symbol.
quiz.a: P_T − P_R = αL + α_c N_c + α_s N_s + M. P_T and P_R are dBm; α is dB/km; L is km; α_c and α_s are dB; N_c and N_s are counts; M is dB.

quiz.q: Why is the system margin added as a loss term instead of being measured at the receiver?
quiz.a: The margin is a reserve for future ageing, temperature, repairs and extra connectors. It is not present in the new link, so it is not measured. Adding it in dB checks that even after those changes the received power stays above sensitivity.

quiz.q: A 1550 nm link has P_T = 1 dBm, P_R = −30 dBm, L = 80 km, α = 0.22 dB/km, N_c = 2 at 0.5 dB each, N_s = 7 at 0.1 dB each, and M = 5 dB. Find the spare margin and state whether the budget closes.
quiz.a: Fiber 80 × 0.22 = 17.6 dB. Connectors 2 × 0.5 = 1.0 dB. Splices 7 × 0.1 = 0.7 dB. Used = 17.6 + 1.0 + 0.7 + 5 = 24.3 dB. Available = 1 − (−30) = 31 dB. Spare = 31 − 24.3 = 6.7 dB. It closes.

quiz.q: An 850 nm multimode link uses 500 m of fiber at 3.0 dB/km, two connectors at 1 dB each, no splices, a 4 dB margin, P_T = −3 dBm and P_R = −20 dBm. Find the spare margin.
quiz.a: Fiber 0.5 × 3.0 = 1.5 dB. Connectors 2 × 1 = 2.0 dB. Used = 1.5 + 2.0 + 4 = 7.5 dB. Available = −3 − (−20) = 17 dB. Spare = 17 − 7.5 = 9.5 dB. The budget closes.

quiz.q: Distinguish receiver sensitivity from receiver overload.
quiz.a: Sensitivity is the minimum power needed for the required bit error rate. Overload is the maximum power before the receiver saturates or distorts. The received power must lie between them.

quiz.q: A design has spare margin −2 dB. Give two changes that would make the budget close, with the approximate dB saved.
quiz.a: Reduce length by 10 km: at 0.22 dB/km this saves 2.2 dB, enough. Or use a source 3 dB stronger: changing 0 dBm to 3 dBm adds 3 dB to available power, also enough. Either change makes the spare positive without cutting the system margin.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, the same arithmetic sits inside a spreadsheet or a vendor tool, but the inputs come from measured fiber, connector and splice data and from a receiver datasheet. Modern long-haul systems add forward error correction coding gain, optical signal-to-noise ratio and per-channel WDM budgets. Search for optical link budget spreadsheet, dispersion power penalty and FEC coding gain to see how the simple sum grows.
